Miguel Martínez drove through the park where he used to walk his daughters in the evening. Their swings were still there, though covered with dust.

Elvira Selzer walked the three blocks from her house to the transit agency office. She'd forgotten her cane at home, and it had been a while since she'd walked, so slowly was the most she could manage. But the transit agency building was an easy ride from the school where she worked as a janitor.

Traffic had been bad this morning, with soccer games in every city park and restaurants full and children getting ready for graduation.

In the agency's front lobby, the young man at the welcome desk caught Ms. Selzer a little teacup of water, and she took him by the arms — the name tag on his lapel read Tomás — as she made her way to the crates of bicycles. He helped her choose and hoisted up the one she settled for, an old brown lady's mountain bike, and he stepped in and out of his tiny office printing the release forms while she sipped her water.

The manager of the bike station was a large man with a red checkered handkerchief in his back pocket, and he helped Ms. Selzer into her seat and adjusted her shoes, and he threw a leash and a nine-millimeter over her shoulder as she pushed away.

Miguel Martínez stepped onto the crowded commuter bus and took a window seat in the back, where he could look up at the green dusty hills in front of him, even if the bus windows were spotted with graffiti. He was nearly forty minutes early to work, but the day was his alone now.

Dolores Ochoa stood on the sidewalk outside the grocery store and understood, for the first time in the years since her son had been deported, that she was alive. For her it was almost a season, this beginning of spring. Both her grandchildren were in high school, and her sister had moved in to help share the mortgage. The grocery was only two blocks away.

Ms. Selzer pedaled through parks and along freshly cut lawns, past elementary and middle and high schools, glancing at the closets full of wall maps that her colleagues had painted during the summer, past midnight playgrounds and statues and fountains splashing in the culverts.

They rode, and were happy.

Dolores took off her glasses, pulled her wet napkin across her eyes, crossed herself, and thanked God aloud. She kept Tomás's number in her phone: every morning, after she punched in the new number, she'd dial him next and let him know the good news. He'd said he wanted to come pick her up and take her to see her family later.

When the items on her to-do list fell short over the next three days, Dolores didn't feel a twitch of annoyance at herself. She'd went to the bank and deposits a check from her power of attorney on Thursday. She canceled her Saturday church committee meeting so she could sleep: the nights were restful and eerily quiet in the apartment when her neighbors weren't leaving. The library was in her way home, so she checked out her usual mysteries.

On Friday, before he picked her up to go to Miami, Tomás gave Dolores a handshake and a kiss on the cheek without her asking for one, and then parked the bus outside her building with the lights on while they hugged through the window. Her son called and asked if she was okay, so Dolores took two more short trips to her room while they talked. He didn't act different from usual, and the visit ended fine, and Tomás came back for her afterwards with a can of spray deodorant from the health fair and a hug. The spray didn't quite get the sweat stains out of her blouse.

In the grocery store Dolores bought frozen chicken patties and frozen peas, everything on her list. Afterwards, Tomás kissed her on the cheek again, and gave her the agency tomorrow's opening hours before she left the hospital. The lady at the front gave her hugs and kisses, too.

Outside, the sky was blank and blue.

Dolores took Tomás's arm—she always stumbled when she came in and out of the hospital—and started, for the first time in nearly three years, toward a bus stop.

At almost the same time Dolores sat at her kitchen table, Olivia parked her van a block from the clinic, stood up from the driver's seat and stretched. It had been a long kind of morning.

The trip down from the city had been fine apart from some fog in the lowlands that had made her stick to twenty, and she'd maybe been a literal minute late to pick up Jacqueline, the first client on the route. Except the next stop was an old white-haired woman sitting on the edge of the sidewalk with half a dozen cardboard boxes around her.

"Hi," Olivia said, "I'm looking for Clara. Do you know where she lives?"

"It's so nice of you to stop," the old woman said, "but Clara's in Millport prison, and this is Dorothy." She handed Olivia two address labels, one typed just a little blurry, one with careful block letters and a chapel name at the bottom. "I live here."

"Thank you so much. And I bet it was nice of someone to take you to the thrift shop. I'll be back for you."

"It's really nothing," Dorothy said, as Olivia jogged for the van.

"Mama Otero was waiting outside the clinic. I only covered two blocks, but the guy next to me was probably Ramon."

"Did he ask you out?"

"He didn't exactly say anything, until I was heading into the clinic, and then he said he liked my van."

"We used to use white vans. They stink. The nicer ones have this blue coating on the inside, but even then the first year they stink."

"Can I meet Clara today?"

"Really no. I talked to her SIR. You can wait inside, if you have something to do around here."

"You could pay for coffee," Leah said, and that was true.

The clinic spread over three floors and about half a city block. Its goal was not to cure mental illness, but to make it possible for people with mental illness to again live as independently as possible; it did not engage in research or long-term studies, although it collaborated with several other agencies to provide services, collect data, and find funding sources. It was growing, mostly because they got more money if they grew, but even so, in the years Olivia had worked with them, they'd had to send people in crisis away once or twice a week. As for the other world she'd grown up in, the one that had used every scrap of that agency's budget — policemen in pump cars pulling drunks off the street; savings tamers siphoning nickel cans out of people's trash — had disappeared some time ago.

Maybe it was all lost and impossible to untangle.

Everything left to solve the problem was so piecemeal. Monday against Thursday. Instead of a plan to fix everything at once, the route was a roundabout for Route 9, an effort to hang on to a speed bump.

She sipped her coffee and got up. The bus stop across the street was close enough she could walk without looking at the schedule. Route 9, in any case, had been interrupted by March Madness.

Soon enough the three months were up. In the airport in Springfield the agency staff got word: Route 9 came within ten rides of the target, 3 percent short, just two dozen people a day too few.

Dolores stood for a long minute on the Capitol Hill Memorial Bridge, looking from the water to the flatlands of Capitol Hill and back. The vista had been one of the first things she noticed when she arrived three years before, a few years ago, and she'd given her husband a wry smile.

"Maybe you're Princeton bound this time round," she told him, and he'd laughed.

She crossed the bridge and caught Tomás waiting at the traffic light. There were only three of them on the bus by then, the younger woman holding a car seat and her purse, the other a man with two boxes of paperwork balanced in his lap.

Dolores sat next to the empty seat and took a long breath.

Tomás rolled up next to her. "Hey, Dolores, how's your job hunt coming?"

She smiled, and as the bus turned down Wright Street, the little morning shoppers and joggers slipping by, she said, "I haven't been looking too hard. It's all diplomas and babble and tests, anyway."

"I hear that."

She started with the first column of numbers—triangles made of white boxes. At the end of March it said 99: the counts for the last few days. It didn't make sense. Then she remembered the Y for yes and the V for no on her voter registration card. Maybe the question was whether she would keep riding the bus. How to Talk to Someone Who's Grieving

Mrs. Spears, age 32

Was you raised by your family

Are all your children boys

Did he leave you a distressing letter

Gloria interviewed Mrs. Spears over the phone because she still didn't feel good and the old woman didn't drive. Mrs. Spears described her son as "kind and prayerful." Did you pray together? What prayer? On your knees? She wanted to know what kind of home the boy had chosen. His wife getting along with the children? Mrs. Spears was silent for a long time. Gloria waited. Mrs. Spears described her other sons. The second son had married a woman who could change tires and had given birth to two living children and one dead child. The third son had been murdered in a convenience store. The fourth was sitting behind his mother making sure she answered the questions right.

Mrs. Spears had known her son's wife long enough to know her brain was always over and over. This was an image the woman thought of on her own, to aid in a faster retrieval of necessary information, as you do with your children. It was a whiteboard. She viewed her thoughts unwriting over a clean white surface. Gloria took this to mean the woman was suffering from various kinds of interference. But one of the things she'd discovered about surviving was you had to be scrupulous about what you judged interference, and what you called a human brain. She asked Mrs. Spears to describe her son as a room or a house. Water pouring in the windows from outside. Did you do that or did it get out? The room or house reached all the way back to his grandparents' home down the road; the boy's mother before her. If you butchered one chicken it was like wrecking twenty crops. A window that opened properly on its weatherstripping but that's all. You might get lost in the house he was from. The boy's wife was trying to put a floor under the room.

Gloria prepared the next call and noticed Mrs. Spears had asked for her own number. She dialed the old woman's landline.

"They ask everybody to tell the same story," Mrs. Spears said.

On January 25, the body of nine-year-old Alice Walton was found in a wooded area near the Middle Fork River, in the Ozark Mountains of northwestern Arkansas. She had been stabbed to death and dumped with her tires removed, a detail that led to numerous reports falsely claimed that she drove a vehicle in the last hours of her life. It is believed that someone with local knowledge lured Alice into a remote area with the promise of the drugs that she and many others seem to think are easily procured there.

A 20-something with straggly blond hair was obscured by a pullover hoodie, and it was hard to tell much of anything else. William stood on the peach-colored tile outside the coffee shop. He'd wanted coffee, but it was too hot even in the shade and nearby the smell of frying pork rinds kept putting the trail of a hazy blue tail in the air. There were empty booths inside, but he didn't have the energy to go in and ask the woman behind the counter to sit him down.

"Why don't you just come in here on out, you ah goin' to catch another half?"

William turned. The man was old and skinny, wearing overalls and a straw sun hat. He sat across from William at the table, and across from him a ninety-year-old woman sat in an armchair, dozing and half-delirious from medication.

William didn't feel up to having a conversation with a stranger, but sometimes you would answer someone to get them to go away, and then they linger anyway. There's something you have to be about them. It's still rude in a considerate way, but at least you won't get hassled for being antisocial.

"I ain't a half human," he said. "What kind ah thing is that supposed ta be?"

"That's what you are. See? If you're gonna tell someone to move you ah need ta be able ta make it out 'em. 'Cause I'm here, and I'm stay here."

The man was conscious, William thought. Not necessarily of what was around him, but conscious.

Dolores stayed up until three reading user posts on the agency's Facebook page. When she went to sleep she could still see the Ride 9 route letters printed on her eyelids.

At the agency headquarters the next morning, some managers talked about how hard it was to hang on to your customers when they were only ninety-six rides a day. That wasn’t even counting the people she’d put on other routes she’d hung on to.

In the director's office, Dolores sat in her favorite chair.

"The service,” she said, “is necessary in Millport."

The director was an older man who had promised the county administrators he'd get the numbers up. His tie was mixing red and brown this morning.

"I’ll tell them," he said. "I'll tell them again. But the people that count here—"

"Oh, yes, the people that count." Dolores said. “You know I was the treasurer? Two years back after the ice storm. The people that count voted in that father of ten over me."

The director snorted, but he seemed pleased that she could figure that much out.

"And you know,” Dolores said, “the paper reported what we averaged every day last month—"

"I’ve read the numbers," he said.

Dolores rolled her eyes, and then said what she wanted. "If they are going to find someplace else to put that route money—because, I’m sure, it’s already budgeted out—well, I’m asking that they put it where they think it can do the most good." She paused to make them think about what that might be, and then said: "In Millport." She folded her hands. After a moment, the director said, slowly: "And if the county people ask, you’ll just tell them to call me themselves. This is one of those times where it’s good to keep the chain of communication to a minimum.”

"I know it is."

"I'll tell them. I'll tell them everyone. You have your ride.” 

Dolores wiped a tear from her cheek. "I know," she said. "I know."

And on the bottom, a white pop-up apologized for the inconvenience, but explained that Route 9 would be discontinued on March 31. Four elderly men in wheelchairs could no longer get their groceries. Two coworkers who lived on different sides of town no longer walked past each other three times a day. A woman who drove her truck to the nearest bus stop twenty miles away no longer rose lurid orange with dawn to deliver food to big greenhouses of marijuana plants.

It wasn't until the last day of Route 9 that anyone realized why. It wasn't because the route was too expensive per hour, and the third shift wasn't spending its budget the right way. The operator had committed financial fraud, embezzling hundreds of thousands of dollars each year — and Route 9, as far as anyone could remember, never missed a payroll.

Three years later, the state investigators and lawyers and forensic accountants were done. Schoolchildren could protect themselves against fraud, if they worked at banks or brokerage houses. The operators and higher-ups at agencies or hospitals were familiar enough with fraud to say, for instance, that there are no dark rouge neckties.

The volunteers who ran Millport's agency neither received nor expected relatively high salaries. The new trips bill never crossed a dotted line to show that it took more money, and even if it did, new trips always took more money at least for a little while. The math of Plan C

There's only so much room on the roads. If I leave now, I can beat the traffic and get to work before eight, but if Mary leaves at the same time she'll spend half her morning in a jam. If they both manage to plan an extra ten minutes in the morning, they're more likely to get to work on time, and to get home on time too. If a bus schedule floats through all this, everyone benefits.

Traffic engineers doing modeling as part of New Jersey Transit's congestion pricing proposal in 2016.

This is a mathematical truism, so straightforward that the governor of Maryland has made congestion pricing a signature issue in a midterm election. It's the premise of the current congestion pricing proposal in San Diego, the one that somehow failed to get on the ballot and has to be revived by special legislation. It even underlies the many, many spell-it-out-any-which-way-through-plaques-and-signs-and-road-work sections of cities that people hate: traffic engineers rarely waste their time cutting lanes for no reason.

The dream program delivers all the benefits of a mathematical truism, but none of the complexity. Since 2007, Sweden and Singapore have used this exact program: if you don't live in the zone, and you come in during rush hour, you pay a fee. (In New York City, congestion pricing is mostly the same thing, except a small sliver of the zone also applies to people who live inside it.)

But unlike Sweden and Singapore: Brooklyn strongly resembles the target areas. And Minneapolis for the same reasons as Seattle.

"I think the Minneapolis and Seattle conversations are different from Boston," says Alan Pisarski, who teaches city planning at MIT and worked for New York City's transportation department on congestion pricing. The discourse around the Boston Circle was almost machiavellian: how do you pick a plan that does the most to fix transportation in the area, even if some of the benefits flow to other parts of the city – like the businesses in Brookline or Back Bay?

New York is caught by that dynamic now: businesses surrounding the congestion-pricing zone have opposed the plan, claiming work meetings or deliveries will have to be made remote. However innocent the opposition's motives, that doesn't make for a healthy debate.

The route to Sun River Senior Apartments wound through the channels left by the old mining roads up in the hills north of town, as the giant old trucks had done back before it was all solar fields and bioelectric tanks. There were bare winding stretches between suburbs full of Tudor-style brick apartments with the names of starts printed on the front: Sirius Village, Vega Court, other names Dolores could never remember. As the bus passed the long curved galleries along the ravines next to the generation plants, someone would be sitting in every one of the dozen or so big armchairs, leaning forward over their tablet or handheld.

They were all waiting for the results of the Route 21 pilot project, started up a few months after Route 9 and taking out a smaller percentage of their Social Security than people in the ninth district had been spending. The difference? They'd given up a twenty-minute wait for a big computerized shuttle that took them all the way across town.

Today the wait would be longer: 7:30 before the first shuttle hit the upper end of the loop.

Dolores tapped Tomás on the shoulder when he got on board. "How many this month, driver?"

She smiled and pulled out a pack of cash, and gave him a folded bill.

Inside, Tomás took out his phone and clicked over to calculate the tip. He'd gotten a lot of those, dolares all, during the winter, as it became clear that Route 9 was going to pass the threshold.

The door hissed open to admit him down from the booth. "Omar," he said. "How many this morning?"

At the other end of the line, a handful of men and women leaned over their tablets or phones, waiting as the numbers from all the regional agencies came in. The usual end-of-training spreadsheet.

Omar handed out the cash, one by one.

Ten minutes later Omar felt someone tap him on the shoulder from behind.".

"I can drive you."

She touched his sleeve. "Put it away."

He turned and saw her. She was an inch shorter than him, with dark hair that looked as carefully styled as his own, cut short and with the faintest suggestion of spike. Her trousers were black and from the corner of his eye they reminded him of stag beetles. Her shoes were white. There was a light mesh purse hanging from her left shoulder.

"You my next stop?" he asked.

The world of Directional Notifications is not very big yet, or very famous. It is designed and managed by a man named Dave, who shares an office with his friend George. They, like so many other businesses that call Seattle home, take up a floor of a building in the Denny Triangle, hometown of Microsoft and current homes to Uber, Amazon, and countless other start-ups. The older tech companies use northwest-corner office space, sometimes augmented by floor plans that look like pieces in Tetris, but Directional Notifications is straightforward and well-lit.

Directional Notifications is just about what the name implies. Unlike Uber or Get with Bob,* which specialize in connecting passenger and driver or passenger and personal assistant, Directional Notifications sends geotagged push notifications to people who are walking too close to either prohibited or unsecured areas. They can range from "Security notice: area to your left, level you are currently on, not secure" to "Call 911, you're about to walk into a shooting vault" to a delightfully sarcastic "Don't worry, you're ok" notification in the event that the incursion in question was entirely imaginary.

*Again, a different ride-share service than the one that gets an actual call-out below.

George and Dave are a little disappointed that maps play a relatively small role, but their software can also guide people away from construction or water main work, and remind them that the mall had a drug bust yesterday, and what-have-you. They prefer to think of themselves as trusty guides stretching into and out of reality, a philosophy that helps them get through the days when they only get one or two emails. The week before Stella moved out I took her to church one last time. She made a show of asking me not to help her when she walked in, but she still took my arm when she got close enough to see that the guest parking was full and her spot in front of the church was taken.

"Lydia, give this woman your spot," I said when I saw Lydia coming up the walk behind us, Luke all the way back in the parking lot with the radio still on. "Stella needs to sit front and center today."

Lydia smiled, but Stella saw how empty the rows were and shook her head. "I'll find something, Faye. I always do."

The bells rang and everyone filtered inside, but Stella lingered in the vestibule with me.

"You seem different today," she said. "More serious."

I took out my pocket change so we wouldn't be holding hands, which would have been a spectacle. "I still do," I said, taking a deep breath. "But this is going to sound crazy coming from an old divide-and-conquer biologist. I think we're good."

Stella blinked.

"Last Monday night..." And I told her about Dolores and her swimming pool and the crooked branches in my cornfield. "I never had more than an impression, but you're right, Stella. You build something anyway. You do the best you can. I still think the Greys saw all of us as nuts, but maybe that only makes us, I don't know, kindred spirits. You hope for a better world, you work to build it, and while you're waiting for whatever comes next, you find happiness in what is."

Stella's mouth fell open. "All this time you thought they were watching you too."

"I just said that," I said.

We sat down side by side, Stella three rows back from where she usually sat. Up front, a spotlight caught the grey enamel of Father Watson's wheelchair and picked out the folds of his robes like a halo of dappled clouds. We were quiet for the next hour, though she didn't hold my hand.

From behind, I heard the rustle of wool, and smelled cedar from the salt jar someone had put in front of Stella as incense.

She had given the flowers to the old woman.

I hadn't appreciated how nice it was until I worked next to her for a year. The penthouse office was a shared space. I was under her sometimes, above her sometimes. Other desks were between us. Mostly I could walk past without seeing, but my desk and hers were close enough that if I tilted my neck just right I could see her work all day.

Until then I had never noticed her walk the entire time she was in the building—or any time she wasn't on her way somewhere. She walked right, left, right, left. She timed it out almost exactly, not accounting for traffic at lunch hours. It wasn't a walk with someone else. We had her schedule cleared by the time we figured it out, and it wasn't meetings or phone calls. And sometimes it was just in a zigzag for 15 minutes before the next section of the walk. She never stopped at the smoking shelter or the food truck; she just walked.

When we saw those emails near the end of the week, we both knew what would happen. It didn't mean much for the investigation—we were lying detective offices at the time. I'm not one to preach about hard work, capital "T" Truth, trust, or justice, but it did bother me something fierce. If someone were skimming money from an account—our client's capital account!—first we'd have to deal with disciplinary meetings as vagrants, then our lack of conduct during our investigation would be at the head of the list.

How glad was I when the new executive came in? I had made almost no progress on the case, but ringing her in to a new job was truly one of the highlights of my life.

At the clinic she got her fingers poked for diabetes and her blood pressure checked. The nurse told her to move the salt, the carbs, and the sugar a notch farther to the down side of the scale. She asked what to do instead. The nurse didn't have anything. If you spend on something, you have to spend less on something else.

Parked outside the doctor's office, Dolores saw the other side of the ledger. The van she'd hitched with the jumper cables was there at the curb, waiting among the specialty buses and the handicapped-accessible vans.

She bought five lottery tickets, the same numbers as last week. She scored her own ticket before she came back to the bus. She was playing the other agency numbers, too. She walked back to the clinic with the spring in her step. Her grandson said they were advertising their routes too much. Either way, she was buying her tickets.

She stepped from the first bus on the route as if onto her own porch. Her body met the air and found that the emotional gear had been shifting as she rode. Just a week ago she had been a subtle participant. She was very much about it. The librarian, who would open the community college center for them, waved to her from the second bus.

When the RV was next on board, the track she walked from the bus to her apartment would be. She didn't need to say it out loud but she did anyway: they left their chance in Memphis.

She printed up a copy of the trial data, took it with her. The bus stop wasn't far from where she usually parked, or from where Tomás stopped every day, so she didn't have to wait. He was there already, wearing the khakis he always had on. He gave her hand a scold, like he always did.

He laughed and asked which church she went to, so she told him.

When he saw what the agency wanted, Zapatero asked if he could borrow a Santiago peach from the blablon and eat it while he studied the data. The postmaster was happy to oblige.

"It's a grapefruit—"

"I know," Ansioncer said.

"A mí," Zapatero said, thinking about Tomás.

"I know. Because of—everything," Zapatero said.

Dolores had Timothy take her up to the fall festival on the town square first thing in the morning, and then make her rounds at the grocery, where the manager knew her, and the clinic, which she could still find by the parking lot left by some old store that had closed.

no comma after "later that week" and "later that week" is the better one. do you agree?
Yes, I agree. The phrase "Later that week" works well as is, with no comma after it. This is standard in modern English usage: introductory time phrases like "Later that week," "That evening," or "The following day" typically take a comma after them if they begin a sentence or clause. However, in this sentence, your construction is actually:

"Later that week, Dolores forwarded the article to her son."

Since "Later that week" begins the sentence and is followed immediately by the main clause, a comma after it would be correct by standard grammar rules. However, many contemporary writers and editors omit the comma if the introductory element is short and the connection to the main clause is clear. Both versions are understandable, but the version with the comma is technically more correct for clarity.

But your sentence, as written in the text, actually does *not* have a comma ("Later that week Dolores forwarded the article...") because you’re following the style of some modern prose that omits the comma after such time phrases when the transition is clear and the sentence structure is simple.

In formal writing or in situations where clarity is paramount, using the comma is safer:
> Later that week, Dolores forwarded the article to her son.

But in modern, more casual narrative writing, as you have it, the comma can be (and often is) omitted. 

So to answer your question directly:  
You can write it either way and be understood, but including the comma after "Later that week" is the stricter grammatical choice. Your version without a comma is perfectly fine for contemporary narrative prose. It’s a minor stylistic choice rather than a clear error. Which to use depends on your style preference and the formality of your writing.

Origin of quote

The passage you’ve referenced is from the short story "Route 9" by Anna Klassen, published in The New Yorker on February 17, 2023.

Summary and context of the quote

This excerpt serves as the poignant conclusion to the story, reflecting on the impact that a simple public transit route had on the life of Dolores Ochoa, an elderly woman who had been isolated after losing her ability to drive. When the temporary bus route was approved and she could once again access her community independently, it wasn’t just a logistical change; it was a lifeline that brought her back into social contact and restored a sense of dignity and purpose.

The final paragraph undergoes a tonal shift from the earlier, more factual recounting of the route's statistics to a deeply personal and emotional understanding of what those numbers meant to a single individual—and by extension, to others in her community who benefited similarly.

Key quotes from the final paragraph:

> "For a month afterward Dolores found herself waiting just inside the door, feeling the morning wind on her face while she waited for the bus that wasn’t coming."

This line elegantly encapsulates the loss Dolores feels when the route is discontinued. The physical act of waiting—performed out of muscle memory and hope— underscores how integrated the route had become in her daily routine and sense of connection. The “bus that wasn’t coming” is both literal and symbolic, representing the fragility of social support and the vulnerability of those dependent on such services.

10,235 rides in ninety-three days. Ridership would "continue to meet the pilot's performance-based metrics," the update read, and the route would be made permanent.

Dolores blinked her watery eyes and leaned in with her magnifying glass. She swallowed hard, the way she did when the pain in her knee flared. It wasn't just that she could get to the restaurant again, she thought. It was that no one even had to think about the money. The bus was hers too.

Later that morning, Dolores made her way to the kitchen table again, her arms full of cans of tomatoes and corn and beans. She reached into the drawer where her sunglasses and her paperbacks lived, and pulled out her pocket Qur'an instead. She flattened it against the table with a can of tomatoes and pressed a thumb through the center of it, right through the verse where Sura VII ended and Sura VIII began, the way she always stopped when she reached the break at the end of a chapter of her life and wondered what the next one would hold.

She had not driven a car in three years. She would not drive a car again. But today was a beginning, not an end, and Dolores rose, set her cans on the counter, and reached for her purse.

"Oh, thank God," Dolores said. She closed her eyes and let the words sit for a moment inside her.

Any ride she wanted, for as long as she wanted, for no more money than she had been paying for one cab trip at a time. She reached for the phone and called her son. "I don't need to borrow your car anymore," she said. "I'm good to go."

Then she called the church social committee and asked if she could help organize a picnic. Everyone could take Route 9.

Art Friedman had wanted to see if the affected people would notice some improvement in their lives, as a justification for directing the county council to spend money to make their lives better. It wasn't enough for the county to fund a thing; that thing had to be seen to be working.

But there was a deeper reason Art had pushed for the survey, back in the meeting over the winter.

Early in his first term as chair of the county council, Art had overseen the cancellation of three low-ridership bus routes in favor of one new route on the other side of the county, where more people could be collected at once. It saved money, but the council chamber had been full of angry faces that night. And although Art knew he hadn't done anything wrong, he felt like he was beginning to understand why it had been so upsetting.

The council was the place where a decision got made. It couldn't be the place where the decision was explained. But sometimes those things blurred together. There was always a human cost, however necessary and reasonable the decision, and the further away a person was from the seat of power, the harder it was to see that the decision had anything to do with trying to help. Art didn't want that to happen again. He wanted the people who relied on a bus route to see clearly that if they made themselves known, if they showed up and spoke and took the survey and rode the bus on the first day and every day, then he would have to listen.

No one could say he hadn't given them the chance.

When the county manager handed him the results, Art saw the route had been kept. One hundred and seven riders a day, maybe a little more or less some days. He highlighted the number in yellow and made a note on the edge of the page:

Actually helped.

He smiled at that. It felt like the beginning of something good.

"It's almost finish line time," her son had texted her. She waited for the web page to load. Her hands trembled.

At 9:03 she opened the text her son had sent again. At 9:04 she looked at the website again and saw that it had not changed.

At 9:05 she heard from two neighbors who had been watching on their own devices and called her excitedly. In the pause between their sentences she could hear a siren in the distance, and she turned down the volume on her phone while she listened.

At 9:06 the number changed on the website. 101 rides a day had become 98.

"Is it definite?" she asked, with the phone still in her hand, and three of her neighbors stood outside her door in their slippers, and one of them answered, "No," but then the number went back up to 101 again, and none of them had an answer for that.

At 9:07 Dolores turned the magnifying glass on the number once more. When it stayed put at 101, she sat down at the kitchen table again, and called her son, who was already at work.

The three neighbors eventually went back to their own apartments. Dolores sat at the table, sipping her coffee until the cup was cold. When someone knocked on her door again it was the man from the transit agency, who brought her a sticker that said thank you for riding route 9.

Later that day the number changed to 97, but she didn't notice until the next morning.

Three paragraphs I liked:

1.  "To keep it, the agency said, the route had to average a hundred rides a day over the trial: nine thousand by the end of March." — "To keep it" as in "to keep the route in operation," as opposed to "to keep (the number of rides) at a hundred." Such an interesting and compressed sentence.

2.  "She told everyone at church about it and helped two women in her building figure out the schedule." — "Figure out the schedule" is such a perfect phrase here. It means "learn how often the bus comes and what times it runs," but it could also mean "discover why the route exists" or "understand the logic behind it." Such a rich and ambiguous phrase.

3.  "The driver on the morning run, a young man named Tomás, learned her name in the first week." — This could be the setup for a later paragraph involving some development with Tomás, or it could just be part of the texture that the author is building — we get to know little things about Dolores's life now that she has this bus route. It's also appropriate that Tomás is described as a "young man," since the bus route probably wouldn't have a driver Dolores's age, and we get a sense of the generational difference, and the community, and yet this isn't used to drum up some pathos or schmaltz. This is just the way things are.

The story is a quiet, small one, but there's a dignity and care here. The point of view is nearest to Dolores but shifts a bit from her to others at moments. The ending is another great sentence: "The Route 9 trial had ended the day before, and it had averaged a hundred and twelve rides a day." It's plain but contains so much by being plain, the matter-of-factness of a goal achieved by the community. Every word of that last sentence does more than one job.

   I would use this story to show students that you don't need huge plot developments or a lot of characters to make a narrative interesting and resonant. So much of the resonance here comes from the accumulation of small details. The fate of the route is tied to numbers, and those numbers come down to Dolores and a few others who make the effort to use it and tell others about it.

"Route 9" is a story by Richard Ford, from his latest short story collection, Let Me Be Frank With You (Eenguin Press). I saw Richard Ford give a reading a few years ago, and afterwards he spoke for a while with the booksellers and audience members who had stayed. Someone asked him what he thought when he sat down to write a story, and he said that he thought about a character who had an emotional need he didn't yet understand, and then he listened to what that character said to him about why they needed that thing. Route 9, its title the only thing on the page, is one of the quietest, most moving stories I have ever read, a story about a small moment in one elderly woman's life, and the way that one small thing can matter so deeply to a person who has seen a lot of loss.

Dolores slid her finger to the article below. The headline said: "Immigrant Driver Keeps Trial Route Alive With Story of His Own."

It had been a tough year for the agency. Late the previous fall an immigrant bus driver had been fired for missing a stop, and the ride-sharing drivers had started organizing in his support. Around the same time, the local paper had come out against special programs for immigrant families, and the mayor had been in a bad mood. The story about Tomás was a way to say that the experiment had been a success in spite of that.

By the time Dolores got through the article, she was crying.

That Tuesday the newspaper ran a follow-up. Because of the success of Route 9, they said, the agency would be adding a Saturday morning route that would make it easier to get to the clinic for Dialysis. There was a picture of Tomás with the manager of the agency, a young woman who had a masters degree in social work. Tomás was smiling widely, and so was the manager. She was wearing a button that said Welcome in eighteen different languages.

This time, Dolores told her grandson about the article, and when it was time for his Saturday visit they rode the new bus route together.

At the clinic, Dolores's son said, "Thank God we don't have to get a ride from my wife anymore."

Dolores smiled at him. "We will see how it goes," she said.

It did go well. Six months later, Route 9 ran six days a week, with two evening runs on Wednesdays for the people who went to classes at the community college.

A lawyer that Dolores had known from the Butterfly House helped the agency change the rules about who could qualify for the shuttle passes.

It wasn't perfect. Some weeks there weren't enough drivers and the evening bus was late. Sometimes there was traffic, or road construction on the highway that made the ride take longer than it should. Dolores and her son would be waiting at the stop when the bus pulled in. He would wave at it. She would stand up, so the driver would see her.

Dolores slid her magnifying glass away from the tablet and pressed her fingers to her lips, which is what she did whenever she was happy.

Based on my extensive extensive experience in writing, this is one of my better efforts. In some ways it could be improved or have gone in a different direction—for instance, if I steered it away from the implication that Dolores would be grateful for the route, and focused it instead on what she would decide to do now that she didn't have to count on rides from her son as much. That's the direction the story might seem to "want" to go in. But it's also useful to write a scene where things go right for a character for no special reason, where small gestures add up and good fortune is just there, not earned.  

Ultimately it's not a question of making better or worse choices as a writer (though I'm eager to keep working on both). It's a question of making the choice that serves the story I want to tell.

In October of 2018, a Democrat named Josh Hawley was elected to the Senate from Missouri. During his campaign, he made it clear that he was opposed to what he called "big government" and to wasting taxpayer money. He told the St. Louis Post-Dispatch that he was going to do his best to cut the funding that the federal government gave to public transit all over the country, and especially to Amtrak. These programs, he said, had been "mismanaged for decades." He added, "If the states want to fund these programs, that's totally fine, but why should the federal government be spending money on ammonia-fueled trains and routes to hockey games?" He went on to say that taxpayer money was often invested in bus routes that averaged fewer than two riders per trip.

Hawley took office in January of 2019. Almost immediately, he announced that Missouri would no longer take advantage of a federal program that gave transit agencies hundreds of millions of dollars every year, in the form of operating and capital grants, to maintain and expand bus and rail systems. Instead, the state would put that money toward highway improvements. Federal law said that if a state declined the highway money that went along with those grants and instead preferred to keep the transit funds, the state could do that, so long as it matched twenty percent of the federal contribution. But accepting federal dollars for transit was anathema to Hawley, who began telling Missourians that his state no longer received a dime from Washington for public transportation.

Confronted with the facts, Hawley doubled down. He insisted that a provision in the law, which allowed the money to be shifted to highway improvements, was tantamount to accepting highway money, therefore Missouri no longer qualified for transit funds. The provision had been in the law since 1982, but until Hawley no governor had tried to interpret it that way. The Federal Transit Administration told him that his reading was incorrect and offered to walk him through the statute. Hawley declined. From the beginning of 2019 through the end of that year, Missouri received no money from the FTA. The state's largest transit agencies calculated that they were losing, in total, more than eight hundred thousand dollars per day.

The 787, and the ship building problem

Airplanes don't come apart the way ships do. Usually you buy an airliner, use it for thirty years, then sell it to an airline somewhere. If you need more or fewer planes, you buy or sell whole aircraft. You don't just buy a new engine for your 747, then buy a new set of landing gear from someone else, and a radar system from someone else, and all your safety equipment from someone else. Without that complexity, the 787 was only moderately different than any other plane program.

That almost didn't happen, though. At the beginning of the program in 2003, the engineers told Boeing that the unforeseen difficulties they would have to solve were too great, and the penalty for failure too heavy. Deliver four airplanes less than one year early, and the initial customers would be out of a business. Deliver four airplanes more than one year late, and they would be out of a business. Even a week off either side of schedule would be a loss of 100 million dollars.

The only way to get enough of the schedule risk out was to have multiple companies working in parallel. That could work with Boeing's smaller planes, with one company contributing engines, and another landing gear, and another a fuselage. But with the 787 size and complexity you wouldn't just buy an engine, you'd need entire companies working independently with their own engineers and staff, writing their own software, and assembling everything themselves only to ship as a complete piece to Boeing. The only time you've seen that kind of complexity in the aerospace industry is when entire ships are made in this way.
